---
title: "Code Sample: Ohio vs. Michigan Accidental Opioid Overdose Diff-in-Diff"
output: 
  pdf_document: 
    number_sections: true

# Background

The purpose of this analysis is to estimate the effect of 7-day opioid
prescription limits announced in March 2017 and effective as of September 2017 
on opioid death rates in Ohio. Since a randomized controlled trial is not 
feasible, to determine the efficacy of the treatment, I employ a
differences-in-differences (DiD) approach to control for time-invariant and
individual-fixed factors that would otherwise bias estimates of treatment 
effects. I model a simple two-group, two-period differences-in-differences
estimation, where Ohio is my treatment group, and the neighboring state of
Michigan is the control group. I consider August 31st, 2017 to be the date of
treatment. The period of interest is November 2016 to June 2018, ten months
before and after treatment, as Michigan's own 7-day prescription limits for the
treatment of acute pain took effect in July 2018.

Throughout this investigation, I will describe my data sources, clean and 
prepare the data for analysis, conduct summary analyses of death rates in both 
the treatment and control groups, evaluate key assumptions for valid DiD 
analyses, fit a DiD model, and discuss the results as well as any limitations of 
the analysis.

# Analysis

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Import Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(scales)
library(readxl)
library(stringr)
library(glue)
library(psych)
library(knitr)

```

## Data
I use the CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death data, restricted to substance
related underlying causes, to compare track opioid death rates in Ohio and 
Michigan in the ten months before and after September 2017.

### Importing and Merging Data
Due to export size restrictions, I exported the data in 2-4 year subsets. Hence,
I import multiple files and merge them below.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

cod_raw <- list.files("/projects/lightcast-mccrary/import/jh_scratch/"
                , pattern = "Multiple Cause of Death"
                , full.names = TRUE) %>%
  map_dfr(read_csv) %>%  # import and combine files in folder
  clean_names() # clean variable names

# view sample of the data and variables available
head(cod_raw)

```

From this data, I have variables indicating state, year, month,
multiple cause of death, underlying cause of death, and number of deaths.

Values appear to be unavailable at the level of the data for population, crude 
death rate, and age-adjusted death rate.

### Investigating Data Quality and Availability

First, I confirm that there are no duplicate observations at the state code, 
month code, multiple cause of death code, and underlying cause of death code 
level, which is a risk I incur when exporting data subsets and re-merging.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# check for duplicates

check_duplicates <- cod_raw %>% 
  select(contains("code")) %>% 
  group_by_all() %>% 
  summarize(ct = n()) %>% 
  filter(ct > 1)

print(check_duplicates)

```
Duplicate observations appear to occur only when the values for all variables
are null. I plan to filter these out in the cleaning step.

Next, I investigate the states and years the data cover.

```{r message=FALSE}

distinct_years <- cod_raw %>% 
  select(year) %>% 
  unique() %>% 
  print()

distinct_states <- cod_raw %>% 
  select(state) %>% 
  unique() %>% 
  print()

```

The data cover 48 states (excluding NA), including Ohio and Michigan, and 11
years (excluding NA) from 2012 to 2020.

Then, I identify how many missing values each variable has.

```{r message=FALSE}

missing_cts <- colSums(is.na(cod_raw)) %>% 
  data.frame() %>% 
  filter(. > 0) %>% 
  print()

```
As expected from the duplicate investigation, each variable has 542 missing
values, except for $\textit{notes}$, which has 31,263 missing values and will
not be used in the analysis anyways.

## Clean and Prepare Data for Analysis

In this next part, I clean and prepare my data for analysis. This includes
1. filtering the data to the states, periods, and death causes of interest, 2.
aggregating deaths across underlying causes, 3. transforming variables as
needed, 4. joining ALFRED state-level population data to calculate death rates,
and 5. creating time and treatment dummies to be used in the diff-in-diff
analyses.

Below, I filter my data to Ohio and Michigan in the periods spanning December 
2016 to June 2018. In addition, I limit underlying causes of death to ICD-10 
underlying cause of death codes X40-X44 and multiple causes of death to 
opioid-related ICD multiple cause of death codes: T40.1, T40.2, T40.3, T40.4,
and T40.6, as is standard* in analyses of accidental opioid overdoses.

*https://ibis.utah.gov/ibisph-view/pdf/resource/query/DrugOverdoseMortalityCodes.pdf

```{r message=FALSE}

cod_clean <- cod_raw %>% 
  mutate(month = as.Date(paste0(year, substring(month_code, 6, 7), "01"), format="%Y%m%d")) %>% 
  filter(
    # filter periods
    month >= "2016-11-01"
    , month <= "2018-06-01"
    # filter groups
    , state %in% c("Ohio", "Michigan")
    # limit to accidental poisoning & opioid-related death codes
    , str_detect(underlying_cause_of_death_code, "^X4[0-4]$")
    , multiple_cause_of_death_code 
        %in% c("T40.1", "T40.2", "T40.3", "T40.4", "T40.6")
    ) %>% 
  mutate(
    state
    , year
    , month
    , multiple_cause_of_death
    , multiple_cause_of_death_code
    , deaths) %>%
  group_by(state, year, month
           , multiple_cause_of_death
           , multiple_cause_of_death_code) %>% 
  # aggregate opioid deaths
  summarize(deaths = sum(deaths)) %>% 
  ungroup()

```

Note that in the above chunk, I aggregated opioid deaths across underlying
causes of death. This does not introduce potential for multi-counting certain
deaths, since each death certificate lists a single underlying cause of death, 
and, thus, the groups are mutually exclusive. However, if I were to aggregate
across multiple causes of death, I would run the risk of double counting deaths,
for more than one multiple cause of death can be associated with more than one
multiple causes of death. In fact, the risk is even high considering the context
of the analysis being drug overdoses, where more than one drug is often found in
a person's system in the event of an overdose. See 
https://wonder.cdc.gov/wonder/help/ucd.html for more information on how
ICD-10 codes map to death certificates.

Furthermore, I inspect the availability of ICD-10 code reporting in Ohio and
Michigan during the analysis period.

```{r}

check_cod_availability <- cod_clean %>% 
  filter(state %in% c("Ohio", "Michigan")) %>% 
  group_by(state, multiple_cause_of_death) %>% 
  summarize(ct = n()) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  print()

```

Reporting on Methadone (T40.3) and Other Unspecified Narcotics (T40.6) is 
limited during the period of analysis period for both states. Though, both Ohio 
and Michigan report death counts for Heroin, Other Opioids, and Other Synthetic 
Narcotics in all 20 periods. If multiple cause of death ICD-10 groups were 
mutually exclusive, I would consider aggregating these groups, however, as 
previously discussed, we can not aggregate without inviting double counting 
risks. Yet more, aggregation poses conceptual risks, as there are meaningful 
differences between these groups that may obfuscate from the true treatment 
effects at a given time. For example, Heroin use often occurs later in the cycle 
of opioid addiction, so changes in Heroin-related accidental drug deaths may 
take longer to appear as a result of an intervention at an initial prescription. 
Also, by forfeiting this variation, I would lose the ability to analyze the role 
of substitution as a continuation of this analysis (i.e. Do prescription caps 
lead those experiencing addiction to substitute Heroin for Other Opioids?).

Thus, I elect to keep the codes disaggregated, but I restrict my analysis to the 
three ICD-10 groups that are completely represented across all periods. 

Now, I join the data to the ALFRED population data. Since the ALFRED
population data is only available by state at the annual-level, I assume linear
population growth to interpolate the state populations in a given month. Note
that the ALFRED population data is referenced to July 1.

```{r}

alfred <- read_xlsx("/projects/lightcast-mccrary/import/jh_scratch/US_population_by_state.xlsx"
                    , sheet = "Annual") %>%
  # add buffer years for lead and lag calculations
  filter(year(observation_date) >= 2015
         , year(observation_date) <= 2020) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = contains("POP")
               , names_to = "state"
               , values_to = "population") %>% 
  transmute(year = year(observation_date)
            , state = state.name[match(str_remove(state, "POP"), state.abb)]
            , population = population*1000) %>% 
  arrange(year) %>% 
  group_by(state) %>% 
  mutate(population_lead = lead(population, 1)
         , population_lag = lag(population, 1))
  
cod_joined <- cod_clean %>% 
  filter(multiple_cause_of_death_code 
        %in% c("T40.1", "T40.2", "T40.4")) %>% 
  left_join(alfred, by = c("year", "state")) %>% 
  # transform population in a month as a weighted average of 
  # the distance between two annual population estimates
  mutate(
    # subtract 7 from month to anchor July as 0
    month_num = as.numeric(month(month)) - 7
          # no change to July population
         , population = case_when(month_num == 0 ~ population
                          # for August-December, weight by distance from 
                          # population estimate in current and next year           
                          , month_num > 0 ~ (month_num*population_lead 
                                        + (12-month_num)*population)/12
                          # for January-June, weight by distance from 
                          # population estimate in current and prior year 
                          , month_num < 0 ~ (-month_num*population_lag
                                        + (12+month_num)*population)/12)
         , death_rate_100k = 100000*deaths/population) %>% 
  select(state
       , month
       , multiple_cause_of_death
       , deaths
       , population
       , death_rate_100k)

```

Then, I add my treatment and control dummies to prepare the data for the DiD
analyses.

```{r}

cod_diff_in_diff <- cod_joined %>%
  mutate(time_dum = if_else(month >= "2017-09-01", 1, 0)
         , treated_dum = if_else(state == "Ohio", 1, 0))

```

# Summary Analyses

## Summary Table of Death Rates

Before performing regression analyses, I pull summary statistics of death rates 
by state, pre- vs. post- treatment, and ICD-10 multiple cause of death codes.

```{r}

death_rate_summary_stats <- cod_diff_in_diff %>% 
  group_by(multiple_cause_of_death, time_dum, state) %>% 
  summarize(n = n()
            , mean = mean(death_rate_100k, na.rm=TRUE)
            , sd = sqrt(mean((death_rate_100k 
                              - mean(death_rate_100k, na.rm=TRUE))^2
                             , na.rm=TRUE))
            , median = median(death_rate_100k, na.rm=TRUE)
            , min = min(death_rate_100k, na.rm = TRUE)
            , max = max(death_rate_100k, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  print()

```
For Heroin-related deaths, it appears that the mean death rate is closer in
magnitude after treatment than before treatment. For Other Opioids and Other 
Synthetic Opioids, this is also true.

I also perform a cursory evaluation of pre-treatment summary statistics.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

pre_trend_investigation <- cod_diff_in_diff %>% 
  filter(time_dum == 0) %>% 
  group_by(multiple_cause_of_death, state) %>% 
  summarize(mean_death_rate = mean(death_rate_100k, na.rm=TRUE)
            , mean_population = mean(population, na.rm=TRUE)
            # calculate death rate linear trend
            , death_rate_slope = (last(death_rate_100k) 
                                  - first(death_rate_100k))/(n()-1)) %>% 
  print()

```

Crucially, upon visual inspection of the numbers, the linear trends of Michigan
and Ohio appear most parallel for Other Synthetic Narcotics. However, I do not 
perform any tests at this point to evaluate the statistical strength of this 
relationship.

# Evaluate Key Assumptions

Some necessary conditions for DiD estimation to be valid include the following:

1. Pre-treatment trends are parallel.

2. The Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) holds.

I perform statistical tests to evaluate item 1 and provide a conceptual
discussion of item 2.

## Assumption 1: Parallel Trends

As a two-group, two-period implementation of a two-way fixed effects model, a
DiD analysis requires that there are no confounding variables that vary with
time and between groups. In other words, parallel trends hold. For example, if 
Michigan were to (and did in fact) expand access to opioid counseling in the 
time between September 2017 and July 2018, then the DiD method would not account 
for this factor and the estimated average treatment effect would be biased 
(omitted variable bias). In a formal research investigation, I would research 
policy and demographic changes and control for any time-varying differences 
between the groups in my regression.

### Trend Visualizations

To verify parallel trends, or, at the very least, not rule them out, I chart
death rates in Ohio and Michigan over time, and perform a visual inspection.

```{r}

chart_input_df <- data.frame(cause_of_death = 
                         c("T40.1" = "Heroin"
                           , "T40.2" = "Other opioids"
                           , "T40.4" = "Other synthetic narcotics"))

chart_ts <- function(cause_of_death){
  
  chart_data <- cod_diff_in_diff %>% 
    filter(multiple_cause_of_death == cause_of_death)
  
  y_min = floor(min(chart_data$death_rate_100k, na.rm = TRUE))
  
  y_max = ceiling(max(chart_data$death_rate_100k, na.rm = TRUE))
  
  timeseries <- 
    ggplot(chart_data
    ) +  
    geom_line(aes(x = month
                  , y = death_rate_100k
                  , color = state
                  , group = state)
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)
                       , breaks = seq(y_min, y_max, by = 0.2)
                       , limits = c(y_min, y_max)
    ) +
    scale_x_date(expand = c(0, 0)
                 , date_breaks = "1 month"
                 , date_labels = "%b %Y"
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2017-09-01")
               , linetype = "longdash"
    ) +
    annotate("text"
             , x = as.Date("2017-09-01")
             , y = Inf
             , label = "Ohio Prescription Limit Effective"
             , angle = 90
             , family = "serif"
             , vjust = -.5
             , hjust = 1
             , size = 3.5
             , color = "black"
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c('Ohio' = '#E41A1C', 'Michigan' = '#254061')
    ) +
    labs(title = glue("Opioid Related Deaths in Michigan vs. Ohio")
         , subtitle = glue("{str_to_title(cause_of_death)}, Nov 2016 - Jun 2018")
         , y = glue("Deaths per 100k")
         , x = ""
    ) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 10)
          , plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 16)
          , plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12)
          , axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1, size = 8)
          , axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9)
          , axis.title.y = element_text(size = 11)
          , legend.position = "bottom"
          , legend.box = "horizontal"
          , legend.title = element_blank()
    )
  
}

charts <- pmap(chart_input_df, chart_ts)

```

```{r}

# Review trends in Heroin-related accidental overdose deaths

heroin_trends <- charts[[1]] %>% 
  plot()

```
Upon visual inspection, trends appear to be generally on par in terms of
Heroin deaths in the period leading up to September 2017. Notably, they seem to
diverge slightly in the few months after prescription limits are effective but
converge around December 2017.

```{r}

# Review trends in Other Opioid-related accidental overdose deaths
other_opioid_trends <- charts[[2]] %>% 
  plot()

```
Trends appear somewhat parallel until January 2017 when they diverge sizeably 
and then dramatically after March 2017. Strikingly, death rates appear to converge 
and then diverge again in the period prior to treatment. Trends appear more 
parallel after treatment than before.

I also notice a spike in Other Opioid death rates in Ohio in April 2017 that
persists for two months until June 2017. There may be some sort of external shock 
that is affecting Other Opioid death rates in this period. In a more expansive 
analysis, I would likely conduct some public research to see if I can explain and 
attempt to control for the factors driving the pre-treatment spike.

```{r}

# Review trends in Other Synthetic Narcotic-related accidental overdose deaths

synthetic_trends <- charts[[3]] %>% 
  plot()

```
Trends in Other Synthetic Narcotic death rates appear somewhat parallel, barring
a few spikes in Ohio's death rate, up until treatment and two months past treatment.
After November 2017, Other Synthetic Narcotic-related death rates begin trending
downward and flattening out. A delayed treatment effect may make sense as this 
category is primarily composed of Fentanyl deaths; Fentanyl is typically used in 
later stages of the course of addiction. There are several sharp spikes that 
indicate there may be a seasonal component to deaths or even reporting of the 
deaths. I considered using an MA(3) transformation of death rates to smooth the 
trend, but, due to concerns about limitations to inference introduced by serial 
correlation in a two-group setting (unable to cluster SE's), I elected to 
continue with raw death rates.

### Statistical Tests of Trends

Now, I perform a simple linear regression test to see if parallel trends are violated. 
In particular, I test whether there is a significant interaction between the month
$\textit{t}$ and group $\textit{i}$ (state) in the pre-treatment period.

The model treats deaths per 100,000 as a linear function of treatment period and 
treatment group (Ohio) dummies as well as the interaction between the two 
dummies:

$$DeathRate100k_{ti} = \beta_0+\beta_1*Month_{t} + \beta_2*Ohio_{i} + \beta_3*Month_{t}\times Ohio_{i}\\ \quad t \in \{1,2,...Treatment\;Month - 1\},\quad i\in\{0,1\}$$

```{r}

model_pre_trends <- function(cause_of_death){
  
  # filter to pre-treatment data
  pre_trend_data <- cod_diff_in_diff %>% 
    filter(multiple_cause_of_death == cause_of_death
           , time_dum == 0) %>% 
    # get time period
    mutate(time_num = match(month, unique(cod_diff_in_diff$month)) - 1)
  
  # evaluate whether we can reject null hypothesis on the interaction
  # between the period and the group: B = 0
  model <- lm(death_rate_100k ~ time_num * treated_dum, data = pre_trend_data)
  
  summary(model)
  
}

pre_trends <- pmap(chart_input_df, model_pre_trends)

```

I am testing $H_0: \beta_3 = 0$ and $H_a: \beta_3 \neq 0$ . If $H_0$ is
rejected, then parallel trends are violated. If I fail to reject $H_0$, then
the outcome of this test is consistent with parallel trends, but it is not
definitive. In particular, failure to reject a null hypothesis does not imply
and acceptance of the alternative hypothesis.

```{r}

heroin_pre_trends <- pre_trends[[1]] %>% 
  print()

```
For Heroin, I reject $H_0$. $\beta_3$ is significant at the 99% confidence 
level (P-Value = 0.002).

```{r}

other_opioid_pre_trends <- pre_trends[[2]] %>% 
  print()

```
For Other Opioids, I fail to reject the null hypothesis. $\beta_3$ is 
insignificant and close to zero.

```{r}

synthetic_pre_trends <- pre_trends[[3]] %>% 
  print()

```

For Other Synthetic Narcotics, I fail to reject the null hypothesis. $\beta_3$ 
is insignificant and close to zero.

Furthermore, I considered an event study approach to pre-testing 
(He & Wang, 2017). Though, it is possible that there are alternative functional 
forms that would output similar pre-trend coefficients but yield substantial 
bias (Roth, 2019).

While I can neither verify or reject parallel trends outright, I continue with 
this assumption for Other Opioids and Other Synthetic Narcotics for the sake of 
the exercise. I recognize the limitations this imposes on the validity of the 
results.

## Assumption 2: SUTVA

An unbiased DiD analysis would require that the composition of the comparison 
groups remain stable over the analysis period. In addition, the treatment of one 
group should not affect outcomes in the other group. In this case, we must 
assume that people did not move in and out of Michigan or Ohio in any way that 
would impact opioid-related death rates. One other essential consideration in
analyses of addiction or any sort of epidemiological question, for that matter,
is whether or not the remaining living population is equally susceptible to
addiction. In other words, if the majority of people who are prone to opioid
addiction or vulnerable to poor prescription practices in Ohio have already died 
of opioid overdoses, then we may see death rates decrease, even though it would
not be a result of the policy intervention. Moreover, spillover effects are
possible, since Michigan and Ohio are neighboring states. Those suffering from
an opioid addiction in Ohio may cross state lines to seek prescriptions if they
are denied their desired quantity. Or, if fewer people are addicted
to opioids in Ohio, producers and sellers of Heroin and Fentanyl may turn to
larger, nearby markets, like Michigan to maintain or increase sales.

Despite the limitations discussed, I proceed with the analysis taking these
assumptions as given for the sake of the exercise.

# Fitting the Differences-in-Differences Model

For illustrative purposes, I derive the average treatment effect (ATE) of opioid
prescription limits using an algebraic and a regression method. Both methods
should yield the same results.

## Algebraic ATE Estimation

Conceptually, the average treatment effect in a DiD model is the difference 
between (between estimator) the difference between the pre- and post- treatment 
means within each group (within estimator).

The ATE is algebraically defined as follows:

$$Average\;Treatment\;Effect = ({Y_{Ohio,\;1}} - {Y_{Ohio,\;0}}) - ({Y_{Michigan,\;1}} - {Y_{Michigan,\;0}}),\quad 1 = On\;or\;after\;September\; 2017$$

```{r}

get_ate <- function(cause_of_death){

yt1 = cod_diff_in_diff %>% 
  filter(treated_dum == 1, time_dum == 1
         , multiple_cause_of_death == cause_of_death) %>% 
  pull(death_rate_100k) %>% 
  mean(., na.rm = TRUE)

yt0 = cod_diff_in_diff %>% 
  filter(treated_dum == 1, time_dum == 0
         , multiple_cause_of_death == cause_of_death) %>% 
  pull(death_rate_100k) %>% 
  mean(., na.rm = TRUE)

yc1 = cod_diff_in_diff %>% 
  filter(treated_dum == 0, time_dum == 1
         , multiple_cause_of_death == cause_of_death) %>% 
  pull(death_rate_100k) %>% 
  mean(., na.rm = TRUE)

yc0 = cod_diff_in_diff %>% 
  filter(treated_dum == 0, time_dum == 0
         , multiple_cause_of_death == cause_of_death) %>% 
  pull(death_rate_100k) %>% 
  mean(., na.rm = TRUE)

treatment_effect = (yt1 - yt0) - (yc1 - yc0)

}

input_df <- data.frame(cause_of_death = 
                         c("T40.2" = "Other opioids"
                           , "T40.4" = "Other synthetic narcotics"))

ate <- pmap(input_df, get_ate)

ate

```

The estimated ATE of the treatment on Other Opioid-related accidental overdose
deaths is -0.24. For Other Synthetic Narcotics, the ATE is -0.68. I interpret 
and discuss these results in the next section.

## Regression ATE Estimation

Now, I fit a regression model to estimate the ATE of the DiD.

$$Death\;Rates\;100k_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1*State_i + \beta_2*Treatment\;Period_j + \beta_3*State_i\times Treatment\;Period_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \; i,j\in\{0,1\}$$

```{r}

get_est <- function(cause_of_death){
  
model_data <- cod_diff_in_diff %>% 
  filter(multiple_cause_of_death == cause_of_death)

model <- lm(death_rate_100k ~ time_dum + treated_dum + time_dum:treated_dum
            , data = model_data)

summary(model)

}

diff_in_diff <- pmap(input_df, get_est)

```


```{r}

lm_other_opiods = diff_in_diff[[1]] %>% 
  print()

```
Like the algebraic representation, $\widehat{ATE} = \hat{\beta_3} = -0.24$, for
Other Opioid-related accidental overdose deaths. This result is significant
at the 99% Confidence Level (P-Value = 0.0013).

Given all necessary DiD assumptions hold, we could conclude that Ohio's 7-Day 
opioid prescription limit for acute pain had the effect of reducing accidental
Other Opioid-related overdose deaths by 0.24 deaths per 100k. 

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

average_post_treatment_pop <- cod_joined %>% 
  filter(state == "Ohio"
         , month >= "2017-09-01") %>% 
  summarize(mean = mean(population, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  pull()

crude_other_opioid <- (ate[[1]]/100000)*average_post_treatment_pop

crude_other_opioid

```

Adjusted for Ohio's average population from September 2017 to June 2018, this 
translates to an average of 28.4 fewer Other Opioid-related deaths per month.

```{r}

ate_lm_synthetic_narcotics = diff_in_diff[[2]] %>% 
  print()

```
Like the algebraic representation, $\widehat{ATE} = \hat{\beta_3} = -0.68$, for
Other Synthetic Narcotic-related accidental overdose deaths. This result is 
significant at the 99.9% Confidence Level (P-Value = 0.0006). 

Given all necessary DiD assumptions hold, we could conclude that Ohio's 7-Day 
opioid prescription limit for acute pain had the effect of reducing accidental
Other Synthetic Narcotic-related overdose deaths by 0.68 deaths per 100k. 

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

crude_synthetic_narcotics <- (ate[[2]]/100000)*average_post_treatment_pop

crude_synthetic_narcotics

```

Adjusted for Ohio's average population from September 2017 to June 2018, this 
translates to an average of 79 fewer Other Synthetic Narcotic-related deaths per 
month.

Both of these results being negative is directionally consistent with what we 
would expect from an intervention intended to decrease opioid deaths.

# Limitations & Discussion

I conclude that, given all assumptions hold for the sake of the exercise, the
causal effects of Ohio's policy intervention on Other Opioid- and Other Synthetic
Narcotic-related death rates were negative and significant. One additional
limitation, which I have not yet discussed, is the fact that Ohio's new prescription
limit policy was announced in March 2017, six months in advance of its effective
date. This means that, in the time leading up to treatment, while not required to
do so, clinicians may have begun complying with these guidelines to align with
professional standards. As a result, the effects of this policy may have spilled
over into these earlier months. This could invalidate the conclusions I drew
from the parallel trends analyses and mean that my ATE estimates I reported are 
biased in such a way that they are smaller in magnitude than the true values.
